strengths: Addresses a practically relevant problem: reducing the cost of estimating integrals involving expensive simulators, combining two well-established tools (multilevel Monte Carlo and Stein-based control functionals).

The proposed MLCF is simple, general-purpose and, unlike prior multilevel control variates (Nobile & Tesei, Geraci et al., Fairbanks et al.) or multilevel Bayesian quadrature, requires no problem-specific expert knowledge and works with unnormalised densities/MCMC samples, which is a genuinely useful property for Bayesian inference.
Provides both an unbiasedness result (Proposition 1) and a per-level variance bound (Theorem 2) giving an O(n^{-tau/d - 1/2}) rate that is faster than MLMC's O(n^{-1/2}) under smoothness.

Empirical illustrations include a real-data Bayesian inference task (Lotka-Volterra with the hare/lynx dataset) and compare under an equal-budget (wall-clock) protocol rather than equal sample size, with sensible baselines (MLMC, CF, MCMC) and multiple repetitions.
weaknesses: Novelty is very incremental: the method is a direct plug-in of the existing control functional estimator into each increment of the standard MLMC telescoping sum. Both Proposition 1 and Theorem 2 follow almost immediately by applying known single-level results (Oates et al. 2017/2019, Wendland Thm 11.13) level-by-level and summing; there is no new technical insight specific to the multilevel setting.

The key question that makes a multilevel method interesting -- optimal sample allocation across levels under a cost constraint, and the resulting overall cost-vs-accuracy complexity theorem (the analogue of Giles' complexity theorem) -- is explicitly deferred to future work. Without it, the paper cannot claim a cost advantage theoretically, and the experiments simply reuse the MLMC-optimal allocation, which is provably suboptimal for MLCF.

The paper self-describes as 'initial work' and reads as a workshop abstract: 5 pages of main text, two small examples, a two-paragraph experimental section, and an appendix with essentially no hyperparameter, kernel bandwidth, or reproducibility details (kernel is only stated to be 'squared-exponential'; no code, no lengthscale selection procedure, no seeds).

The theory does not match the experiments: the appendix concedes that 'some of the assumptions are not fulfilled' (e.g. A1 compact box domain vs. R^2/R^8, A5 boundary condition), and the 8-dimensional Lotka-Volterra example is precisely the regime where the m^{-tau/d} rate gain is negligible. The claimed faster rate is therefore not empirically verified anywhere (no convergence-rate plots vs n, only absolute error at three budgets).

Evaluation is weak: only two toy/small examples, very small sample sizes (e.g. 2-6 samples at the finest level, which makes the top-level CF essentially meaningless), no error bars/quantitative tables (results only as box plots), no statistical significance assessment, and no ground-truth description for the Lotka-Volterra reference value.

No comparison to the most directly related prior method, multilevel Bayesian quadrature (Li et al., 2023), on the ODE example where it is applicable; the paper dismisses competitors as 'very difficult or not feasible' without demonstrating this.

The O(m^3) cost of the Stein kernel solve and the cost of gradient evaluations of log pi (which for a posterior involving an ODE solve can be comparable to the integrand cost) are dismissed in one sentence and appear to be excluded from the budget accounting, potentially biasing the equal-budget comparison in favour of MLCF.

Presentation issues: Theorem 2's variance is conditional on X^0 yet the MSE discussion treats it as the unconditional MSE; Remark 1's simplified estimator is biased but the bias is never analysed or bounded even though it is what appears to be used in practice; Tables 1 and 2 have duplicated 'l = 1' column headers; Eq. (1) contains a typo (k(x,y) instead of k(x,x')); several grammatical errors ('Baysian', 'to simply the equations').
